claim: Plutella xylostella is the most widespread Lepidopteran pest species, causing losses of US$ 4–5 billion per year.
source: Plutella xylostella (L.) is the most widespread Lepidopteran pest species, causing losses of US$ 4–5 billion per year (You et al., 2020; Zalucki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (You et al., 2020; Zalucki et al., 2012).

claim: P. xylostella has developed resistance to the usual insecticides because of its short life cycle (14 days).
source: It has developed resistance to the usual insecticides because of its short life cycle (14 days) (Furlong et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Furlong et al., 2013.

claim: P. xylostella mainly selects Brassica species as its host plants.
source: P. xylostella mainly selects Brassica species as its host plants, and its females pat the leaf surfaces with their antennae before egg laying (Qiu et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 1998.

claim: P. xylostella females pat the leaf surfaces with their antennae before egg laying.
source: P. xylostella mainly selects Brassica species as its host plants, and its females pat the leaf surfaces with their antennae before egg laying (Qiu et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 1998.

claim: Sinigrin and brassinolide have relatively higher concentrations in Brassica than in many other plant species.
source: Among these compounds, sinigrin and brassinolide (BL) have relatively higher concentrations in Brassica than in many other plant species (Fahey et al., 2001; Lv et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fahey et al., 2001 and Lv et al., 2014.

claim: Sinigrin is a feeding/oviposition stimulant for P. xylostella.
source: Sinigrin is known to be a feeding/oviposition stimulant for P. xylostella (Gupta and Thorsteinson, 1960).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta and Thorsteinson, 1960.

claim: The medial sensilla styloconica in the maxillary galea of P. xylostella larvae contain a GSN sensitive to sinigrin and other glucosinolates.
source: The medial sensilla styloconica in the maxillary galea of P. xylostella larvae contain a GSN sensitive to sinigrin and other glucosinolates (van Loon et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Loon et al., 2002.

claim: BL is a ubiquitous plant hormone that has been widely studied in relation to its role in plant growth and development.
source: BL is a ubiquitous plant hormone that has been widely studied in relation to its role in plant growth and development (Clouse and Sasse, 1998), but little is known about its effects on the behavior of phytophagous insects.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: Little is known about the effects of BL on the behavior of phytophagous insects.
source: BL is a ubiquitous plant hormone that has been widely studied in relation to its role in plant growth and development (Clouse and Sasse, 1998), but little is known about its effects on the behavior of phytophagous insects.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: 67 GR sequences were validated in P. xylostella (61 GRs from the genome, 3 GRs from the transcriptome, and 3 GRs from GenBank).
source: We obtained 79 annotated GRs (69 GRs from the genome, 7 GRs from the transcriptome, and 3 GRs from GenBank). After removing repetitive sequences and deleting paired sequences with amino acid identity greater than 99%, we validated 67 of the GR sequences (61 GRs from the genome, 3 GRs from the transcriptome, and 3 GRs from GenBank) (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of genomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: The TPM value of PxylGr34 was much higher than those of other GR genes in the antennae, head and forelegs of adults, as well as the mouthparts of larvae.
source: Intriguingly, the TPM value of PxylGr34, which clustered with bitter GRs, was much higher than those of other GR genes in the antennae, head and forelegs of adults, as well as the mouthparts of larvae (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: PxylGr34 was originally annotated from genomic data.
source: PxylGr34 was originally annotated from genomic data (Engsontia et al., 2014), and then detected in the antennal transcriptomic data of P. xylostella (named as 'PxylGr2' in Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Engsontia et al., 2014 and Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The protein encoded by PxylGr34 is typical of most GRs with seven transmembrane domains.
source: The protein encoded by PxylGr34 is typical of most GRs with seven transmembrane domains, and a full open reading frame (ORF) of 418 amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PxylGr34 has a full open reading frame (ORF) of 418 amino acids.
source: The protein encoded by PxylGr34 is typical of most GRs with seven transmembrane domains, and a full open reading frame (ORF) of 418 amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of PxylGr34.

claim: High levels of PxylGr34 transcripts were detected in the larval head.
source: The high levels of PxylGr34 transcripts were detected in the larval head. They were also detected in the larval thoracic legs and gut (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PxylGr34 transcripts were also detected in the larval thoracic legs and gut.
source: The high levels of PxylGr34 transcripts were detected in the larval head. They were also detected in the larval thoracic legs and gut (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In adults, PxylGr34 transcripts were restricted to the antennae.
source: In the adults, PxylGr34 transcripts were restricted to the antennae (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34 at a concentration of 10–4 M.
source: Among 24 tested phytochemicals belonging to sugars, sugar alcohols, amino acids, amines, glucosinolates, and plant and insect hormones (Key Resources Table), BL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34, as did its racemate EBL at a concentration of 10–4 M (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: EBL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34 at a concentration of 10–4 M.
source: Among 24 tested phytochemicals belonging to sugars, sugar alcohols, amino acids, amines, glucosinolates, and plant and insect hormones (Key Resources Table), BL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34, as did its racemate EBL at a concentration of 10–4 M (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The currents induced by BL increased from the lowest threshold concentration of 10–4 M in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The currents induced by BL increased from the lowest threshold concentration of 10–4 M in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C and Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Oocytes expressing PxylGr34 showed weak responses to methyl jasmonate and allyl isothiocyanate.
source: Oocytes expressing PxylGr34 showed weak responses to methyl jasmonate and allyl isothiocyanate, but no response to 20-hydroxyecdysone and other tested compounds (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Oocytes expressing PxylGr34 showed no response to 20-hydroxyecdysone and other tested compounds.
source: Oocytes expressing PxylGr34 showed weak responses to methyl jasmonate and allyl isothiocyanate, but no response to 20-hydroxyecdysone and other tested compounds (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Water-injected oocytes failed to respond to any of the tested chemical stimuli.
source: As negative controls, the water-injected oocytes failed to respond to any of the tested chemical stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lateral sensilla styloconica had no response to BL and EBL.
source: Of the two pairs of sensilla styloconica in the maxillary galea of 4th instar larvae, the lateral sensilla styloconica had no response to BL and EBL (Figure 4A,B,C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 4A, B, C, and D.

claim: The medial sensilla styloconica exhibited vigorous responses to BL and EBL at 3.3 × 10−4 M.
source: the medial sensilla styloconica exhibited vigorous responses to BL and EBL at 3.3 × 10−4 M, and the spike amplitudes induced by BL and EBL were about the same (Figure 4A,B,C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 4A, B, C, and D.

claim: The spike amplitudes induced by BL and EBL were about the same.
source: the medial sensilla styloconica exhibited vigorous responses to BL and EBL at 3.3 × 10−4 M, and the spike amplitudes induced by BL and EBL were about the same (Figure 4A,B,C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 4A, B, C, and D.

claim: The medial sensilla styloconica exhibited vigorous responses to sinigrin.
source: As previously reported, the medial sensilla styloconica also exhibited vigorous responses to sinigrin.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental observations and previous reports.

claim: The spike amplitudes induced by sinigrin were larger than those induced by BL and EBL.
source: However, the spike amplitudes induced by sinigrin were larger than those induced by BL and EBL (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 4E and F.

claim: BL and EBL activate the same neuron, while sinigrin activates a different neuron in the sensillum.
source: These results suggest that BL and EBL activate the same neuron, while sinigrin activates a different neuron in the sensillum.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing different spike amplitudes.

claim: The medial sensilla styloconica showed a dose-dependent response to BL.
source: The medial sensilla styloconica showed a dose-dependent response to BL, although the testing concentrations were limited because of the low solubility of BL in water (highest concentration approximately 3.3 × 10−4 M) (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The feeding areas of larvae were significantly smaller on the leaf discs treated with BL and EBL at concentrations of 10−4 M and above than on the control leaf discs.
source: In a dual-choice feeding test with 4th instar larvae, the feeding areas of larvae were significantly smaller on the leaf discs treated with BL and EBL at concentrations of 10−4 M and above than on the control leaf discs.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data.

claim: The feeding preference of larvae to BL and EBL tended to decrease with increasing BL and EBL concentrations.
source: In addition, the feeding preference of larvae to BL and EBL tended to decrease with increasing BL and EBL concentrations (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that both BL and EBL function as feeding deterrents to P. xylostella larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both BL and EBL function as feeding deterrents to P. xylostella larvae.
source: In addition, the feeding preference of larvae to BL and EBL tended to decrease with increasing BL and EBL concentrations (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that both BL and EBL function as feeding deterrents to P. xylostella larvae.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the feeding preference data showing decreased feeding on BL and EBL-treated discs.

claim: Significantly fewer eggs were laid on the sites treated with BL at 10−4 M, 10−3 M, and 10−2 M than on the control sites.
source: In a dual-choice oviposition test with mated females, significantly fewer eggs were laid on the sites treated with BL at 10−4 M, 10−3 M, and 10−2 M than on the control sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice oviposition assay data.

claim: The oviposition preference tended to decrease as the BL concentrations increased.
source: In addition, the oviposition preference tended to decrease as the BL concentrations increased (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice oviposition assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The relative transcript level of PxylGr34 in the head of larvae treated with PxylGr34 siRNA was half that in the head of larvae treated with GFP siRNA or ddH2O.
source: The relative transcript level of PxylGr34 in the head of larvae treated with PxylGr34 siRNA was half that in the head of larvae treated with green fluorescent protein (GFP) siRNA or ddH2O (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Feeding with siRNA is an effective method for RNAi-inhibition of PxylGr34 in the larval head.
source: This confirmed that feeding with siRNA is an effective method for RNAi-inhibition of PxylGr34 in the larval head.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the qPCR data showing reduced PxylGr34 transcript levels after siRNA treatment.

claim: The medial sensilla styloconica of PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae still showed some response to BL.
source: As shown in Figure 8, although the medial sensilla styloconica of PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae still showed some response to BL, the frequency of spikes to BL elicited in the medial sensilla styloconica of the PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae was decreased (Figure 8B and Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: The frequency of spikes to BL elicited in the medial sensilla styloconica of the PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae was decreased.
source: As shown in Figure 8, although the medial sensilla styloconica of PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae still showed some response to BL, the frequency of spikes to BL elicited in the medial sensilla styloconica of the PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae was decreased (Figure 8B and Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: Both the water-treated larvae and the GFP siRNA-treated larvae preferred control leaf discs over those treated with BL.
source: As shown in Figure 9, both the water-treated larvae and the GFP siRNA-treated larvae preferred control leaf discs over those treated with BL, whereas the PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae showed no significant preference (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae showed no significant preference between control leaf discs and those treated with BL.
source: As shown in Figure 9, both the water-treated larvae and the GFP siRNA-treated larvae preferred control leaf discs over those treated with BL, whereas the PxylGr34 siRNA-treated larvae showed no significant preference (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi attenuated the electrophysiological responses of the medial sensilla styloconica to BL.
source: Thus, the knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi attenuated the electrophysiological responses of the medial sensilla styloconica to BL, and alleviated the deterrent effect of BL on the feeding of P. xylostella larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data from RNAi-treated larvae.

claim: The knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi alleviated the deterrent effect of BL on the feeding of P. xylostella larvae.
source: Thus, the knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi attenuated the electrophysiological responses of the medial sensilla styloconica to BL, and alleviated the deterrent effect of BL on the feeding of P. xylostella larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data from RNAi-treated larvae.

claim: PxylGr34 is specifically tuned to BL and its racemate EBL.
source: Our results show that PxylGr34 is specifically tuned to BL and its racemate EBL, and that the medial sensilla styloconica of 4th instar larvae have electrophysiological responses to BL and EBL.
evidence: The claim is supported by oocyte expression and electrophysiological data.

claim: BL inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition of P. xylostella.
source: Our results also show that BL inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition of P. xylostella, and that knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi can attenuate the responses of sensilla to BL, and abolish the feeding inhibition effect of BL.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding and oviposition assay data.

claim: Knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi can attenuate the responses of sensilla to BL.
source: Our results also show that BL inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition of P. xylostella, and that knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi can attenuate the responses of sensilla to BL, and abolish the feeding inhibition effect of BL.
evidence: The claim is supported by tip-recording data from RNAi-treated larvae.

claim: Knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi can abolish the feeding inhibition effect of BL.
source: Our results also show that BL inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition of P. xylostella, and that knock-down of PxylGr34 by RNAi can attenuate the responses of sensilla to BL, and abolish the feeding inhibition effect of BL.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-choice feeding assay data from RNAi-treated larvae.

claim: This is the first study to show that an insect can detect and react to this steroid plant hormone.
source: This is the first study to show that an insect can detect and react to this steroid plant hormone.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings.

claim: PxylGr34 is a bitter GR specifically tuned to BL.
source: The results of the systematic functional analyses of the GR, the electrophysiological responses of the sensilla, behavioral assays, and behavioral regulation in vivo show that PxylGr34 is a bitter GR specifically tuned to BL.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including oocyte expression, electrophysiology, and behavioral assays.

claim: PxylGr34 mediates the deterrent effects of BL on feeding and ovipositing behaviors of P. xylostella.
source: This receptor mediates the deterrent effects of BL on feeding and ovipositing behaviors of P. xylostella.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing that knock-down of PxylGr34 abolishes BL-induced feeding inhibition.

claim: The larvae of Lepidopteran species have two pairs of gustatory sensilla (medial and lateral sensilla styloconica) located in the maxillae galea.
source: The larvae of Lepidopteran species have two pairs of gustatory sensilla (medial and lateral sensilla styloconica) located in the maxillae galea; these sensilla play a decisive role in larval food selection (Dethier, 1937; Schoonhoven and van Loon, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dethier, 1937 and Schoonhoven and van Loon, 2002.

claim: These sensilla play a decisive role in larval food selection.
source: The larvae of Lepidopteran species have two pairs of gustatory sensilla (medial and lateral sensilla styloconica) located in the maxillae galea; these sensilla play a decisive role in larval food selection (Dethier, 1937; Schoonhoven and van Loon, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dethier, 1937 and Schoonhoven and van Loon, 2002.

claim: Each sensillum usually contains four GSNs, of which one is often responsive to deterrents.
source: Each sensillum usually contains four GSNs, of which one is often responsive to deterrents.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about insect gustatory sensilla.

claim: Ishikawa described a 'deterrent neuron' in the medial sensillum styloconicum of silkworm, Bombyx mori, that responds to several plant alkaloids and phenolics.
source: Ishikawa, 1966 described a 'deterrent neuron' in the medial sensillum styloconicum of silkworm, Bombyx mori, and showed that it responds to several plant alkaloids and phenolics (Ishikawa, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishikawa, 1966.

claim: The tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, has a deterrent neuron in the medial sensillum styloconicum that responds to aristolochic acid.
source: For example, the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, has a deterrent neuron in the medial sensillum styloconicum that responds to aristolochic acid, and another deterrent neuron in the lateral sensillum styloconicum that responds to salicin, caffeine, and aristolochic acid (Glendinning et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glendinning et al., 2002.

claim: The tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, has another deterrent neuron in the lateral sensillum styloconicum that responds to salicin, caffeine, and aristolochic acid.
source: For example, the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, has a deterrent neuron in the medial sensillum styloconicum that responds to aristolochic acid, and another deterrent neuron in the lateral sensillum styloconicum that responds to salicin, caffeine, and aristolochic acid (Glendinning et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glendinning et al., 2002.

claim: The diversity of GRs facilitates the detection of, and discrimination among, a wide range of diverse taste stimuli.
source: The diversity of GRs facilitates the detection of, and discrimination among, a wide range of diverse taste stimuli, implying that different sets of bitter GRs are expressed in these neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the function of GR diversity.

claim: Different sets of bitter GRs are expressed in deterrent neurons.
source: The diversity of GRs facilitates the detection of, and discrimination among, a wide range of diverse taste stimuli, implying that different sets of bitter GRs are expressed in these neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diversity of GRs and their functional roles.

claim: One GSN in the medial maxillary sensillum styloconicum of the 4th instar larvae of the diamondback moth responds to sinigrin.
source: In this study, we proved that one GSN in the medial maxillary sensillum styloconicum of the 4th instar larvae of the diamondback moth responds to sinigrin (van Loon et al., 2002), and we identified one neuron responding to BL and EBL in the same sensillum.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data and a citation to van Loon et al., 2002.

claim: One neuron responding to BL and EBL was identified in the medial maxillary sensillum styloconicum.
source: In this study, we proved that one GSN in the medial maxillary sensillum styloconicum of the 4th instar larvae of the diamondback moth responds to sinigrin (van Loon et al., 2002), and we identified one neuron responding to BL and EBL in the same sensillum.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' electrophysiological data.

claim: For P. xylostella larvae, sinigrin is a feeding stimulant whereas BL and EBL are feeding deterrents.
source: For P. xylostella larvae, sinigrin is a feeding stimulant whereas BL and EBL are feeding deterrents, together with sinigrin and BL/EBL have different spike amplitudes, we speculate that the GRs tuned to sinigrin and BL/EBL are located in different GSNs in the medial sensilla styloconica.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' behavioral assay data.

claim: The GRs tuned to sinigrin and BL/EBL are located in different GSNs in the medial sensilla styloconica.
source: For P. xylostella larvae, sinigrin is a feeding stimulant whereas BL and EBL are feeding deterrents, together with sinigrin and BL/EBL have different spike amplitudes, we speculate that the GRs tuned to sinigrin and BL/EBL are located in different GSNs in the medial sensilla styloconica.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the different spike amplitudes and behavioral effects of sinigrin versus BL/EBL.

claim: The GR family is massively expanded in moth species.
source: The GR family is massively expanded in moth species, and most of the GRs are bitter GRs (Cheng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2017.

claim: Most of the GRs in moth species are bitter GRs.
source: The GR family is massively expanded in moth species, and most of the GRs are bitter GRs (Cheng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2017.

claim: Gr33a mutant flies could not avoid non-volatile repellents like quinine and caffeine.
source: For example, Gr33a mutant flies could not avoid non-volatile repellents like quinine and caffeine (Moon et al., 2009), and mutation of Gr98b impaired the detection of L-canavanine (Shim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moon et al., 2009.

claim: Mutation of Gr98b impaired the detection of L-canavanine.
source: For example, Gr33a mutant flies could not avoid non-volatile repellents like quinine and caffeine (Moon et al., 2009), and mutation of Gr98b impaired the detection of L-canavanine (Shim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shim et al., 2015.

claim: When the bitter GR PxutGr1 of P. xuthus was knocked-down by RNAi, the oviposition behavior in response to synephrine was strongly reduced.
source: When the bitter GR PxutGr1 of P. xuthus was knocked-down by RNAi, the oviposition behavior in response to synephrine was strongly reduced (Ozaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ozaki et al., 2011.

claim: Knock-out of the bitter GR BmorGr66 in B. mori larvae resulted in a loss of feeding specificity for mulberry.
source: Knock-out of the bitter GR BmorGr66 in B. mori larvae resulted in a loss of feeding specificity for mulberry (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: BL and EBL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34.
source: In this study, BL and EBL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34, knock-down of PxylGr34 in the larvae of P. xylostella eliminated the feeding deterrence of BL, indicating that this bitter GR is specifically tuned to BL and EBL, and mediates the aversive response of larvae to BL and related compounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by oocyte expression data.

claim: Knock-down of PxylGr34 in the larvae of P. xylostella eliminated the feeding deterrence of BL.
source: In this study, BL and EBL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34, knock-down of PxylGr34 in the larvae of P. xylostella eliminated the feeding deterrence of BL, indicating that this bitter GR is specifically tuned to BL and EBL, and mediates the aversive response of larvae to BL and related compounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi and behavioral assay data.

claim: PxylGr34 mediates the aversive response of larvae to BL and related compounds.
source: In this study, BL and EBL induced a strong response in the oocytes expressing PxylGr34, knock-down of PxylGr34 in the larvae of P. xylostella eliminated the feeding deterrence of BL, indicating that this bitter GR is specifically tuned to BL and EBL, and mediates the aversive response of larvae to BL and related compounds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the oocyte expression and RNAi data.

claim: The ligands of PxylGr34 could be more than BL and EBL.
source: Although the 24 tested compounds represent a wide range of compound profiles, the ligands of PxylGr34 could be more than BL and EBL.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the limited number of compounds tested.

claim: PxylGr34 could function together with other GRs to perceive other compounds.
source: Given the high expression level of PxylGr34 in the taste organs of P. xylostella, we could not rule out the possibility that this gene also functions together with other GRs to perceive other compounds.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the high expression level of PxylGr34.

claim: BL was the first brassinosteroid (BR) hormone to be discovered in plants.
source: BL was the first brassinosteroid (BR) hormone to be discovered in plants.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the history of BR discovery.

claim: BL was first isolated and identified from a crude extract of pollen from oilseed rape (Brassica napus L.).
source: It was first isolated and identified from a crude extract of pollen from oilseed rape (Brassica napus L.), and was found to induce rapid elongation of pinto bean Phaseolus vulgaris internodes distinct from gibberellin-mediated stem elongation (Mitchell et al., 1970; Grove et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 1970 and Grove et al., 1979.

claim: BL was found to induce rapid elongation of pinto bean Phaseolus vulgaris internodes distinct from gibberellin-mediated stem elongation.
source: It was first isolated and identified from a crude extract of pollen from oilseed rape (Brassica napus L.), and was found to induce rapid elongation of pinto bean Phaseolus vulgaris internodes distinct from gibberellin-mediated stem elongation (Mitchell et al., 1970; Grove et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 1970 and Grove et al., 1979.

claim: Almost all plant tissues contain BRs.
source: Almost all plant tissues contain BRs, and they function to promote elongation and stimulate cell division, participate in vascular differentiation and fertilization, and affect senescence (Clouse and Sasse, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: BRs function to promote elongation and stimulate cell division, participate in vascular differentiation and fertilization, and affect senescence.
source: Almost all plant tissues contain BRs, and they function to promote elongation and stimulate cell division, participate in vascular differentiation and fertilization, and affect senescence (Clouse and Sasse, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: As a C28 BR, BL exhibits the highest activity among all BRs.
source: As a C28 BR, BL exhibits the highest activity among all BRs and is distributed widely in the plant kingdom, along with other biosynthetically related compounds (Clouse and Sasse, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: BL is distributed widely in the plant kingdom, along with other biosynthetically related compounds.
source: As a C28 BR, BL exhibits the highest activity among all BRs and is distributed widely in the plant kingdom, along with other biosynthetically related compounds (Clouse and Sasse, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: Exogenous application of BL and its analog 24-epibrassinolide (EBL) to plants has been shown to increase their stress resistance.
source: Exogenous application of BL and its analog 24-epibrassinolide (EBL) to plants has been shown to increase their stress resistance (Clouse and Sasse, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clouse and Sasse, 1998.

claim: Plant hormones play a key role in regulating plant growth, development, and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses.
source: Plant hormones, although generally found in small amounts and rarely toxic, play a key role in regulating plant growth, development, and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses (Bari and Jones, 2009; Krouk et al., 2011; Wu and Baldwin, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bari and Jones, 2009; Krouk et al., 2011; Wu and Baldwin, 2010.
